title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth LARGEST element in the array. Note this is the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct element — duplicates count. Can you do better than sorting the whole array?
blurb: The selection problem — a size-k min-heap gives O(n log k), and Quickselect gives O(n) average by partitioning around a pivot without fully sorting.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Confirms kth largest counts duplicates (not kth distinct), clarifies 1-indexed k, and recognizes full sorting is O(n log n) — the prompt invites something better.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Reaches at least the size-k min-heap (O(n log k)); ideally proposes Quickselect (O(n) average) and explains the partition-and-recurse-one-side insight versus quicksort recursing both sides.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Heap: keeps exactly k largest by popping when size exceeds k; the root is the answer. Quickselect: maps kth largest to the (n-k)th index in ascending order (or partitions descending), recurses only the side containing the target index, and terminates when pivot lands on it.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: Heap O(n log k) time / O(k) space. Quickselect O(n) average (n + n/2 + n/4 ... = 2n) but O(n^2) worst case; random/median-of-medians pivot mitigates. Full sort O(n log n)/O(1).

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean partition routine (Lomuto or Hoare), in-place swaps, correct index arithmetic for the target rank, no off-by-one in the heap size check.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: k=1 (max) and k=n (min), all-equal elements (partition must still terminate), array of length 1, negative numbers, duplicates around the pivot, k out of range validation.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests duplicates (e.g. [3,3,3,3], k=2 -> 3) and both extremes of k; for Quickselect, reasons about the all-equal worst case for partition.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains the average-case linear recurrence for Quickselect and the O(log k) heap tradeoff, and when a heap is preferable (streaming / k << n / worst-case guarantee).

constraints: Duplicates are allowed; kth largest counts them (not kth distinct)

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: [6,5,4,3,2,1]; the 2nd largest is 5. Equivalently, index n-k = 4 in ascending order.
Sorted descending: [6,5,5,4,3,3,2,2,1]; the 4th element is 4. Duplicate 5s each occupy a rank.

test_cases.expected: 3 — all equal; duplicates count and partition must still terminate
3 — general Quickselect case; verify recursing only one side

reference.optimal_time: O(n) average (Quickselect); O(n log k) if using a size-k heap
reference.optimal_space: O(1) in-place for Quickselect (O(log n) recursion), O(k) for the heap

approaches.name: sort and index
approaches.idea: Sort ascending and return nums[n-k] (or sort descending and return nums[k-1]). Trivially correct and often the right pragmatic choice, but does more work than needed by fully ordering the array.
approaches.space: O(1) to O(n) depending on the sort

approaches.name: size-k min-heap
approaches.idea: Maintain a min-heap of the k largest seen so far. Push each element; if the heap grows beyond k, pop the smallest. After processing all elements the heap's root (minimum of the top k) is the kth largest. Great for streaming data or when k << n, and gives a worst-case bound.

approaches.name: optimal average: Quickselect
approaches.idea: Target rank is index target = n - k in ascending order. Randomly pick a pivot, partition so smaller elements sit left and larger right, and let p be the pivot's final index. If p == target, nums[p] is the answer. If p < target recurse on the right part, else the left part — only ONE side, unlike quicksort. Average work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n). A random (or median-of-medians) pivot avoids the O(n^2) worst case on sorted/adversarial input.
approaches.time: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst (O(n) with median-of-medians pivot)
approaches.space: O(1) extra, O(log n) recursion (or iterative)

follow_ups: Streaming / online version — KthLargest class with an add(val) that returns the current kth largest; the size-k min-heap is the natural fit and add is O(log k).
Return the k largest ELEMENTS (not just the kth) — heap or a single partition around rank n-k then take the right side (order not guaranteed).
Guarantee worst-case O(n) — median-of-medians pivot selection; discuss why it is rarely used in practice (large constant).
kth SMALLEST — symmetric; target index becomes k-1 or invert the comparison.
Median of an array (k = n/2) or kth largest across a data stream that doesn't fit in memory (external / reservoir + heap).
reference.reference_solution:
Quickselect: findKthLargest(nums, k): target = len(nums) - k  // kth largest == (n-k)th smallest, 0-indexed. lo, hi = 0, len(nums)-1. while lo <= hi: p = partition(nums, lo, hi)  // returns pivot's final index. if p == target: return nums[p]. elif p < target: lo = p + 1. else: hi = p - 1.

partition(nums, lo, hi): swap(nums, random(lo, hi), hi)  // randomize to dodge sorted-input worst case. pivot = nums[hi]; i = lo. for j in range(lo, hi): if nums[j] < pivot: swap(nums, i, j); i += 1. swap(nums, i, hi); return i  // pivot now at i, everything left is < pivot.

Iterating instead of recursing keeps space O(1). Heap alternative: min-heap h; for x in nums: heappush(h, x); if len(h) > k: heappop(h). return h[0]. The heap version is O(n log k) but shines for streams and when k is small. Randomizing the pivot is the key robustness step — on already-sorted input a fixed last-element pivot degrades to O(n^2).
pitfalls: Index arithmetic: kth largest is index n-k ascending; off-by-one here is the most common bug.
Recursing into BOTH partitions (that's quicksort, O(n log n)) instead of only the side containing the target.
Fixed pivot (first/last) causing O(n^2) on sorted or all-equal input — randomize or use median-of-three/medians.
Partition not terminating or looping on all-equal arrays — ensure the pivot index always progresses.
Heap version: comparing sizes with the wrong inequality and keeping k+1 or k-1 elements.

interviewer_notes: The prompt's 'can you do better than sorting?' is deliberate — reaching the O(n log k) heap is the mid baseline; proposing Quickselect and articulating the recurse-one-side idea is the strong signal. Let them pick; if they only offer sorting, ask about a streaming feed to nudge them toward a heap, then ask 'can you avoid the log factor entirely?' to surface Quickselect. Watch the index mapping (n-k) closely — hand them nums=[3,2,1,5,6,4], k=2 and ask which index they select. Stay silent through the partition, but if they use a fixed pivot, ask what happens on already-sorted input to elicit randomization. The all-equal array [3,3,3,3] is a great termination test — offer it if they don't. If they nail Quickselect, escalate to the streaming KthLargest class (heap) and, for staff-level, median-of-medians for a worst-case O(n) guarantee and why it's seldom used.
